context: Current closing price of Occidental Petroleum (OXY): $58.81 USD as of 2026-05-25.
justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift from what I assumed was a current price level near 58.9, with gentle appreciation over time. At the one-day horizon, the estimate is essentially anchored to the current price with minimal expected movement, as short-term price action in most financial instruments tends to be dominated by noise rather than trend. Over one week, I applied a slight upward bias reflecting whatever underlying directional momentum or fundamental backdrop was present at the time of the forecast. At one month, the continued small upward drift reflects a longer-run mean-reversion or trend assumption, though the signal becomes increasingly diluted by uncertainty at that horizon.

The confidence interval widths widen substantially as the horizon extends, which reflects the standard square-root-of-time scaling of uncertainty combined with the accumulation of unknown future events. At one day, the interval is tight because most of the randomness that could materialize over a full day is relatively bounded under normal market conditions. By one week, the range expands to reflect several trading sessions worth of potential volatility, news events, and liquidity fluctuations. At one month, the interval nearly spans a 17-point range, reflecting the genuine difficulty of forecasting prices over that timeframe when macro data releases, central bank communications, and shifts in market sentiment can all compound.

Specific risks that could push outcomes outside my stated intervals include sudden macroeconomic shocks such as unexpected inflation prints, central bank policy surprises, or geopolitical escalation that triggers broad risk-off or risk-on repositioning. A liquidity crunch or flash crash event could send prices well below my lower bounds in a matter of hours. On the upside, a strong positive catalyst — such as a policy pivot, better-than-expected earnings or economic data, or a short squeeze dynamic — could push prices well above the upper end of even the one-month interval.

It is also worth acknowledging that my intervals may be somewhat underconfident at the tails, particularly for the one-month horizon. Black swan events are by definition underrepresented in historical volatility estimates, so realized outcomes in extreme macro environments could fall meaningfully outside a 90% confidence interval built on recent historical data. I would treat the one-month interval especially as a central tendency guide rather than a hard bound.
